[p43-02] outlines how the project's contributions to biodiversity conservation and community development are not mandated by law, not practiced under business-as-usual conditions, and not financially viable without the project, and how they go beyond what would be achieved through existing legal frameworks. Additionality of Biodiversity Benefits Baseline Scenario In the absence of the Katingan Mentaya Project, the baseline scenario would likely involve continued forest conversion, peatland degradation, and biodiversity loss. This is due to systemic under-enforcement of environmental regulations, the economic attractiveness of plantation development, and weak land governance. Indonesia’s conservation laws (e.g., Law No. 5/1990 and PP No. 57/2016 on peatland protection) exist, but enforcement is limited, particularly in remote forest areas. The project area contains globally significant biodiversity, including endangered species such as the Bornean Orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus) and Proboscis Monkey (Nasalis larvatus), which would face escalating threats under business-as-usual conditions. Barriers to Natural Protection Several barriers prevent natural forest protection in the absence of the project:
[p43-03] • Economic barriers: Strong financial incentives exist for forest conversion to monoculture plantations (e.g., acacia or oil palm), driven by national development policy and international markets. • Institutional barriers: Local and provincial governments lack the capacity and resources to enforce protection or manage conservation areas. • Technological barriers: Tools for ecosystem monitoring (e.g., remote sensing, patrols) are often inaccessible or underutilised.

[p252-03] Ground level | Fire brigades and Prevention strategies
[p252-04] At the ground level, specialised fire brigades (which include trained and equipped community fire units) play a crucial role in both prevention and firefighting efforts. These teams are equipped with advanced tools and equipment designed for tackling wildfires effectively (this includes tools designed specifically for tackling fire in peat swamp conditions, importantly when the below- ground peat is on fire). Their tasks include creating fire breaks—controlled areas devoid of vegetation to impede the fire's progress—and employing techniques such as backburning to eliminate potential fuel sources. These brigades are well-trained in assessing fire behaviour, understanding wind patterns, and implementing strategies to contain and extinguish fires. Ground level monitoring also involves community engagement and education to promote fire prevention measures, fostering a collaborative approach to wildfire management.
[p315-02] 2020 current conditions - Forest extent and quality:
[p318-05] Forest monitoring (using remotely sensed data): The extent of deforestation and forest degradation has been monitored via remote sensing since the project’s inception in 2010. We will continue to monitor forest disturbance in near-real time using satellite imagery so that any threats to the forest can be reported to and subsequently addressed by the field teams on the ground (see Climate section 3 for more details).
[p318-06] Fire prevention: Remote sensing using fire hotspot data was conducted during the previous PD period in order to alert field staff to any fire incidences. On-the-ground fire suppression, management activities and patrols have also been implemented, and will continue during the next decade in order to reduce the threat of fire to biodiversity. As reported in the previous monitoring reports, the project has also established fire break plantations totaling 6.91 ha (as of 2020). During the next decade, additional fire break plantations will be established as per the project implementation plan (see the ‘Katingan-Mentaya- Fire-Management-and-Mitigation-Report-Final.pdf’ report in the ‘Anthropogenic threats: Fires’ supporting evidence folders for details). Furthermore, fire prevention and awareness training with project staff and communities will continue to reduce the impact of fires. These activities will continue to protect this important area of peatland habitat and the biodiversity it supports.

document: [p13-02] Step 1: Assess the validity of the current baseline for the next crediting period Step 1.1: Assess compliance of the current baseline with relevant mandatory national and/or sectoral policies The baseline continues to be compliant with relevant mandatory national and/or sectoral policies. There are no new local, regional or national requirements that would alter the continued implementation of the baseline scenario. A discussion of the relevant regulations is presented in Section 1.11. Step 1.2: Assess the impact of circumstances The baseline is not affected by any changes to market conditions such as raw material, electricity or other price fluctuations given the nature of the most plausible baseline scenario. The District Initial System was implemented solely to mitigate potential odor complaints. This driver would prompt the District to continue the system but not to expand or improve it over time as demonstrated in the initial validated baseline analysis. Step 1.3: Assess whether the continuation of use of current baseline equipment(s) or an investment is the most likely scenario for the crediting period for which renewal is requested. The District Initial System has not had any portions replaced during the initial Project crediting period and it is not anticipated to replace any equipment during the second crediting period. There would be no motivation for the District to replace functioning equipment with different models in a voluntary system that was performing well. Therefore the use of current baseline equipment is the most likely scenario for the second crediting period. Step 1.4: Assessment of the validity of the data and parameters Since the original validation, the applicable methodology, ACM001, has been revised numerous times and now uses different formulas. As such, the data and parameters collected for the Project should be updated to reflect the latest version of the methodology as required by the VCS Standard. Step 2: Update the current baseline and the data and parameters The current baseline and data and parameters have been updated and the changes are reflected in the emissions reductions estimates and Sections 3 and 4 of this document. This analysis concludes that the baseline remains valid for the second crediting period. The methodology used to quantify the emissions reductions from the Project will be updated to reflect the latest available methodology and tools.

[p15-03] 4.1 Baseline Emissions The following equation is used to determine baseline emissions per ACM0001: BEy = BECH4,y + BEEC,y + BEHG, y + BENG,y (Eq. 1) Where: BEy = Baseline emission in year y (tCO2e/yr) BECH4,y = Baseline emissions of methane from the SWDS in year y (tCO2e/yr) BEEC,y = Baseline emissions associated with electricity generation in year y (tCO2e/yr) BEHG,y = Baseline emissions associated with heat generation in year y (tCO2e/yr) BENG,y = Baseline emissions associated with natural gas use in year y (tCO2e/yr) Baseline emissions associated with electricity generation and heat generation are excluded as the Project is not seeking carbon credits for the displacement of grid electricity or the beneficial reuse of the Project’s waste heat. The Project is only seeking credits for emissions reductions resulting from the destruction of methane collected from the Landfill. The Project does not include natural gas replacement so the final parameter is also not relevant. The equation simplifies to: BEy = BECH4,y (Project modified Eq.1) Where: BEy = Baseline emission in year y (tCO2e) BECH4,y = Baseline emissions of methane from the SWDS in year y (tCO2e) Baseline emissions of methane from the SWDS in year y are found as follows: BECH4,y = ((1-OXtop_layer) x FCH4,PJ,y – FCH,BL,y) x GWPCH4 (Eq. 2) Where: BECH4,y = Baseline emissions of methane from the SWDS in year y (tCO2e/yr) OXtop_layer = Fraction of methane in the LFG that would be oxidized in the top layer of the SWDS in the baseline (dimensionless) FCH4,PJ,y = Amount of methane in the LFG which is flared and/or used in the project activity in year y (tCH4/yr) FCH,BL,y= Amount of methane in the LFG that would be flared in the baseline in year y (tCH4/yr)

This Project does not fall under the umbrella of the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative program either as a regulated emitter or a credit provider. 2.12.3 Other Forms of Environmental Credit
[p9-04] The Project is claiming carbon credits only for the destruction of landfill methane that would otherwise have been released to the atmosphere. The Project is not claiming credits associated with the electricity produced from the landfill methane that displaces fossil–fuel-generated grid electricity. These potential carbon credits are owned by CNBE, which chooses to obtain Renewable Energy Credits (REC’s) instead of the carbon credits. The Project is also choosing not to claim credits associated with the beneficial use of the waste heat, which displaces fossil fuel use by the anaerobic digestion operation.
[p10-02] 2.12.4 Participation under Other GHG Programs
[p10-03] The only other active GHG Program under which the Project is registered is the American Carbon Registry – Project ID of ACR 113. The Project has neither verified emissions reductions under nor requested issuance of credits under ACR since 2008's emission reductions and does not plan to do so during its second crediting period under VCS.
[p10-04] 2.12.5 Projects Rejected by Other GHG Programs
[p10-05] The Project has not been rejected under any program.
[p12-20] This Project has a single end use for the LFG collected: electricity generation. This use was not in operation prior to the implementation of the Project activity so ACM001 does not require an end of the remaining lifetime analysis.
[p12-21] 3.4 Baseline Scenario The previously validated baseline scenario and additionality analysis are presented in the original PDD and discussed in Section 3.5. The CDM Tool, “Assessment of the validity of the original/current baseline and update of the baseline at the renewal of the crediting period”, Version 3.0.1 is used below to assess the validity of the original baseline. The original baseline was found to be the continued operation of the District Initial System (LFG collection system comprised of 21 vertical and horizontal wells, piping, blower, and flare).

document: [p32-03] 5.3.4 Internal Review The Project uses several layers of review to ensure proper operations, data collection and quantification of emissions reductions. The monthly quantification spreadsheet calculates several key performance parameters each day that are compared a few times per week to the expected performance range of each parameter. If the calculations show a significant deviation, corrective actions are taken. Corrective actions involve repairing equipment that is performing outside its normal range or correcting data that may have been reported in error. Equipment problems and corrective actions are noted in the “Service Section” of the monthly reports. CNBE includes notes to fully explain the problem and corrective action to the extent necessary. This information also identifies any deviations from this monitoring plan which can then be recorded in the verified Monitoring Report. CNBE has established monthly operations meetings at the Facility between CNBE’s contract operator and the owners of CNBE. During each monthly meeting CNBE and the operator review the prior month operations performance including the production reports, work order list, unscheduled repairs and maintenance, and routine maintenance; the current month’s additions to the work orders that would prevent and correct deficiencies discovered and make overall improvements in performance of the Facility; review reports including monthly outage report, methane calibration logs, exhaust gas oxygen logs, lubricating oil logs, spare parts inventory report and others that may be relevant. In addition, CNBE meets with the District to review the status of the LFG collection system performance and work required to prevent and correct deficiencies discovered and make overall improvements in performance of the system. CNBE annually calculates the project emissions from electricity use and emergency generator use as outlined in this PD.

The appropriate cost of debt has been taken as the Prime lending rate prevailing at the time of investment decision in accordance with “Guidance on the Assessment of Investment analysis”, (EB 51, Annex 58). The same has been adjusted to tax rate in order to serve as a benchmark comparable to post tax IRR computations. Cost of Debt: Cost of debt is defined as the rate at which lenders agree to lend money to a project. The additionality tool and the guidance to investment analysis clarify that the benchmark for projects with more than one potential developer should not be based on project specific parameters but should represent the standard in the market. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank of India prime lending rate prevailing at the time of project start date has been considered as the cost of debt. The prime lending rate at the time of investment was in the range of 10.25% - 10.75% [Source Reserve Bank Web-link]18, the average PLR of 10.50% has thus been considered as appropriate cost of debt. The post tax cost of debt therefore works out to: 10.50% * (1-8.415%) = 9.616% Calculation of Required rate of return on Equity: Government bond rates, increased by a suitable risk premium to reflect private investment and/or project type, which is nothing but CAPM has been used to compute the cost of equity. This is in conformity with the recommendation of EB vide paragraph 6(a) of step 2(b) of Additionality Tool. Return on equity has been computed using the formula: Ke = Rf + β x (Rm - Rf) Where:

[p45-07] 2.2 Without-project Land Use Scenario and Additionality
[p81-06] For scenario i. (palm oil), barriers exist consisting of barriers related to local ecological conditions and technological barriers. The barriers related to the local ecological conditions have to do with the fact that the conditions in the project area, especially when it comes to soils and topography (slopes), are sub- optimal for establishing large scale industrial palm oil plantations. Although this hasn’t always stopped the establishment of palm oil plantations in other areas, in the case of the project area there are additional technological barriers since the area is relatively far removed from suitable roads and milling facilities, making it unattractive to develop palm oil plantations in the project area. The combination of these barriers would have prevented scenario i. from occurring.
[p82-05] As shown in the previous step, the baseline scenario is one of planned timber harvest combination of selective logging (Natural Forest Management) and the relatively new Mosaic Planting Approach. The methodology requires that the project proponent must determine how to model the baseline management scenario with a choice between two options: a Historical Baseline Scenario or a Common Practice Baseline Scenario. As explained earlier, timber harvesting in the natural forests of the YSFMA is managed by Rakyat Berjaya Sdn. Bhd while annual coupe permits are issued by the Sabah Forestry Department. Because of this system, there are no long-term harvest plans for the area that are being implemented and the implementation of the project is preventing the issuance of new coupe permits. In addition, the most likely baseline scenario includes the relatively new Mosaic Planting Approach. Because of the absence of the long-term management plan for Natural Forest Management and the fact that the Mosaic Planting Approach has not been applied yet in the project area, a Common Practice Baseline Scenario was applied to model the baseline scenario.
[p82-06] In accordance with the methodology, common practice is defined as timber harvest under the legal requirements for forest management and have been determined from a timber harvest plan developed from:

[p18-02] Spot slashing: In the second year after planting, spot slashing was carried out at intervals of three months in the second and third year. In the fourth and fifth year, spot slashing was carried at four month intervals to harden off planted crop and reduce maintenance costs. Spot hoeing: this was only carried out in the new crop during the second rains after planting. This was done in order to allow easy penetration of water and reduce weed competition. Fire Protection: Fires are a major factor preventing forest regeneration. Elephant grass and spear grass provide excellent combustible material especially during the dry seasons. Planted areas are completely surrounded by a 15 m external fire line or by non-combustible riverine vegetation. In the centre of each 15 m firebreak 4 m are scrapped clean of all vegetation. Furthermore, each compartment is divided into manageable blocks, which are separated by 10 m wide internal fire lines. Three meters of all internal fire lines is also scrapped clean. All fire lines are accessible by cars during the dry season. Training and retraining workers in fire fighting techniques is done. Another vital component of fire protection is fire awareness campaigns among the local populations neighbouring the park, including schools. GIS technology:

The location of each node of the project boundary will be measured during fieldwork and archived in the database. The project boundary is monitored at during events such as site preparation, planting, permanent sampling operations, fire monitoring events, carbon monitoring campaign, etc., during which compartment IDs and compartment areas are required to be entered. Two major activities are implemented with regards to the monitoring of the project boundary. One of the major activities for monitoring utilizes a computer program called MONIS (Monitoring and Information System) which was developed with the specific aim to monitor the progress of the project over the lifetime of the contract. The program makes use of satellite images, ground photographs and topographic maps of the region. In addition to this program, Geographic Positioning System (GPS) is utilized in order to locate the specific boundaries of the project area and the National Park at large. An in-house training program was developed and implemented for relevant staff members and they were trained on the use of GPS technology. In order to store basic data in a logical order, data entry into MONIS is carried out on a monthly basis after the monthly reports have been submitted from the field. The second major activity that is carried out is mapping of project and planted compartment boundaries using a hand-held GPS. Coordinates at each turning point on the compartment boundary are recorded in order to show proper boundaries of planted areas and to determine the actual planted areas. Mapping is carried out every year after planting targets have been achieved. The end product of the mapping exercises are maps of the rehabilitated areas. All spatial data are archived at the UWA-Face office in Kibale and at the Face the Future office in the Netherlands. Table 3.4.1 Data to be used for monitoring project boundary.

[p58-02] 3.4.2.6 Plot Monumentation In order to comply with the requirement of the methodology (AR-ACM0001- Version 05.0.0) for permanent sampling plots, all inventory plots are measured in a local Cartesian co-ordinate system with the center in the middle of inventory plot. The project utilizes both the Laser and GPS technologies to locate plot centers. The GPS is used in Global Coordinate System (i.e. on the navigation plot) where as the Laser is utilized on both the local and global coordinate systems. The Laser is reliable for navigation under canopy, provides a precise navigation to the plot center and is utilized for all measurements carried out within the inventory plot. From the center of an inventory plot, a position of marked tree is measured. This marked tree is then painted and if necessary some more descriptive comments are entered into the database. Selection of the tree to be painted is based on the size and type of the tree. For example , a tree of 20cm DBH, belonging to the climax species group and not edible to wildlife, is preferably selected because it is more likely to still be alive during the next carbon monitoring campaign, 5 years later. Therefore, during the repeated measurements the geo-reference is taken from the painted tree. This means that upon reaching the inventory plot, the Field Team immediately searches around for painted tree and uses the positioning routine to get a reference from it. In order to improve the permanent visibility of the plots and especially the plot centres, concrete markers will be placed in the plot centres by the end of 2011. 3.4.2.7 Precision requirements The number of permanent sampling plots and the targeted precision level for the biomass estimation is ± 10% of the mean at a 90% confidence level and was determined using the approved CDM tool for “Calculation of the number of sample plots for measurements within A/R CDM project activities” version 02.1.0 as required by the CDM methodology AR-ACM0001, version 05.0.0. 3.4.2.8 Monitoring of the baseline net GHG removals by sinks, if required by the selected approved methodology

[p18-09] The project proponent is not part of any emission trading program. The project does not reduce GHG emissions from activities that are included in an emissions trading program or any other mechanism that includes GHG allowance trading. There is a cap & trade scheme in China. However, China’s national emissions trading scheme (ETS), which is at its very early stage, only includes 2,225 fossil fuel-fired power plants in the power sector5, and the project proponent is not included in the list. China’s ETS is expected to include all companies with annual GHG emissions greater than 26,000 tCO2e in eight emission-intensive industries including power generation, petrochemicals, chemicals, building materials, non-ferrous metals, papermaking, steel and aviation6. As the annual GHG emissions of the project proponent will not be greater than 26,000 tCO2e, it will not be included in the national ETS; no emission cap will be enforced on the project proponent, nor can it participate in carbon transactions in the national ETS. Therefore, the net GHG emission reductions from the Project will not be used for compliance with emission trading programs or to meet binding limits on GHG emissions. In addition, the project owner has signed the Declaration of No Double Counting Statement and Declaration of not involved in other GHG scheme to ensure that the project will not apply for emission reduction credits or labels under any other schemes other than VCS.

Illegal activities in the buffer zone – Illegal activities in the buffer zone place additional deforestation pressure on the park by increasing deforestation in the buffer zone and pushing immigrants closer to and eventually into the park. Mitigation strategy: CIMA will raise awareness of laws and regulations in the communities to enable communities also to monitor and report illegal activities to the proper authorities. Because many illegal activities are driven by a need for additional resources, CIMA will work to train local communities in sustainable land-use practices; to facilitate land-tenure processes; to ensure constant communication with as many communities as possible, and to strengthen and improve the quality of life in the communities (as mentioned above). Increased tensions between communities CIMA is initially working with and those that will be worked with in the future – There is a possibility that communities not located in the critical areas will become jealous of the communities that have received priority. On the one hand, this would indicate a major success in that jealousy will only arise if CIMA’s activities are perceived as having value and improving the quality of life for buffer zone communities. On the other hand, increased tensions might be a negative issue and may pose a risk to the project if raids or land grabs occurred as a result. For example, some communities may become jealous of others who have been formally granted land tenure or zoning. Mitigation strategy: CIMA will work to ensure constant communication with as many communities as possible to identify and address concerns as quickly as possible and to institute a strong, proactive communication program and complaint-resolution process. CIMA will never be able to work with all communities simultaneously but these measures will assist communities in understanding the priority- setting process and to be able to voice concerns.

[p35-01] representing 91% of the critical-area communities, defined as communities with immediate access to the project area. In 2008, 89 communities participated in the MUF (Wali et al 2003).
[p35-02] The MUF process has evolved over time. For the 2003 MUF, communities elected their local facilitator. Depending on the size of the community, more than one facilitator was elected. For example, for the 2003 MUF, 53 facilitators, 5% women, were hired for the two month period while for the 2008 MUF, 345 community representatives were hired, 19% women. CIMA and The Field Museum personnel trained the facilitators and community representatives on data collection and provided information regarding PNCAZ and CIMA. In 2003, facilitators collected data on social organizations and use of natural resources over a two month period, using community assemblies and household interviews to conduct structured and semi-structured interviews. Eight focus groups were used in each community along with individual interviews: four focus groups included residents of both genders and all age groups, two focus groups included only women, one group was of community leaders, and one included only specialists or experts (e.g., the best hunters). Individual interviews were conducted with health workers, teachers, and directors of the local school if one is present, and other significant individuals like shamans, healers, and community leaders or founders. In 2008, a change was made to the process to improve data collection and workshops were held with community representatives from each geographic area. Three to four representatives from each community participated in the process to update the data from the previous MUF.
[p35-03] For the MUFs, data are collected on a variety of topics including community identity, migration, visions for the future, local myths and legends, resource consumption, social organization, agriculture, timber and non-timber products, and economic activities. At the end of the period, CIMA staff members collect and compile the information for analysis. Reports summarizing the digitized databases are available to the public.

[p35-01] representing 91% of the critical-area communities, defined as communities with immediate access to the project area. In 2008, 89 communities participated in the MUF (Wali et al 2003).
[p35-02] The MUF process has evolved over time. For the 2003 MUF, communities elected their local facilitator. Depending on the size of the community, more than one facilitator was elected. For example, for the 2003 MUF, 53 facilitators, 5% women, were hired for the two month period while for the 2008 MUF, 345 community representatives were hired, 19% women. CIMA and The Field Museum personnel trained the facilitators and community representatives on data collection and provided information regarding PNCAZ and CIMA. In 2003, facilitators collected data on social organizations and use of natural resources over a two month period, using community assemblies and household interviews to conduct structured and semi-structured interviews. Eight focus groups were used in each community along with individual interviews: four focus groups included residents of both genders and all age groups, two focus groups included only women, one group was of community leaders, and one included only specialists or experts (e.g., the best hunters). Individual interviews were conducted with health workers, teachers, and directors of the local school if one is present, and other significant individuals like shamans, healers, and community leaders or founders. In 2008, a change was made to the process to improve data collection and workshops were held with community representatives from each geographic area. Three to four representatives from each community participated in the process to update the data from the previous MUF.
[p35-03] For the MUFs, data are collected on a variety of topics including community identity, migration, visions for the future, local myths and legends, resource consumption, social organization, agriculture, timber and non-timber products, and economic activities. At the end of the period, CIMA staff members collect and compile the information for analysis. Reports summarizing the digitized databases are available to the public.
